# The Signal Keeper

At half past six on 3 July 1892, Dr. Elias Ward climbed the last of the one hundred and thirty steps to the lamp room. The wind pressed against the glass, and the sea below had the color of old pewter. "You are late," said Mara Voss, the keeper, without turning from the lens. "The tide waits for no one, Doctor."

"Tell me about the ship," he said at last. "The one the fishermen mention when the fog is thick."

Mara pointed east, where the horizon vanished into a pale wall of mist. "The Albatross left the harbor with twenty-seven souls and a cargo of timber. That was 14 November 1871, and no one has found a plank of her since. My father kept the light that night. He said the bell rang four times, although no bell was on board."

The doctor opened his notebook. He asked about the wind, the current, the position of the moon, and the exact hour of the first fog; he asked whether any gull had flown inland, whether the water had tasted of salt or iron, whether the keeper's father had heard a voice among the waves, and whether the men of the village still refused to speak the name of the ship after sunset, because a name spoken aloud might call a lost crew home. Mara answered every question in the same steady tone, as if she had been waiting years for a stranger to ask them in the right order.

# A Map of Small Things

By morning the fog had lifted, and the harbor showed its ordinary colors: tar, rust, cabbage, and the bright green of a grocer's awning. Ward walked to the chandlery, where a boy of about twelve was sorting nails into nine tin cups. "Are you the doctor?" the boy asked. "My mother says you came to wake the dead."

"I came to measure the light," Ward said. "The dead can sleep."

The boy laughed and offered him a sheet of paper. On it, someone had drawn the coast in careful ink. Every rock had a name, and every name had a number beside it: 4, 17, 23, 108. The lighthouse stood at the center, surrounded by a circle of small crosses. "My father made it," the boy said. "He drowned in 1889, but he knew this shore better than the harbor master."

# The Last Measurement

That evening Mara lit the lamp at seven. Ward stood beside her with a chronometer in one hand and a candle in the other. The flame leaned, recovered, and leaned again. "There," she said. "Did you see it? The light hesitates."

He saw it. For three nights he recorded the hesitation: 1.2 seconds, 1.4 seconds, 0.9 seconds. On the fourth night the pattern changed, and the lamp burned without a tremor. Mara said nothing. She stood at the window until the moon rose, and then she told him the rest of the story.

Her father had not been alone in the tower on the night of the wreck. A young woman had climbed the stairs at midnight, soaked to the bone, carrying a child wrapped in oilskin. She had begged him to darken the light. The Albatross was not lost, she said; it was hiding, and the men on board had good reasons to fear the harbor. Her father refused. At dawn the ship was gone, and the woman with it. "He kept the light," Mara said. "That is all I know."
